body.text: India’s existing electronic warfare (EW) infrastructure represents decades of sustained investments by the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) and is considerably more capable than public commentary typically acknowledges. The Samyukta ground EW system can deploy across a 100-km-by-70-km operational area for surveillance, interception, direction-finding, and jamming of communications and radar signals. The Samudrika naval EW programme has delivered seven modern systems, including the Shakti shipborne suite inducted on front line naval vessels since 2021.

For the air domain, the Swayam Raksha Kavach airborne EW suite for Tejas Mk1A is undergoing flight-testing and targeted for deployment by the end of 2026. DRDO’s counter-drone portfolio now includes the jammer anti-unmanned aerial vehicle (anti-UAV) system, which detects drone signals across standard frequencies and carries both jamming and spoofing capabilities, enabling the broadcast of false global navigation satellite system signals to mislead drones rather than merely blocking them.

Private sector capability has augmented this DRDO baseline. The IG T-Shul Pulse handheld counter-drone jammer, ordered by both the Army and the Navy, provides directional jamming across a 2 km range in a fully indigenous, scalable production configuration. Zen Technologies has developed an AI-powered counter-unmanned aircraft system combining radar, radio frequency analysis, electro-optical sensors, multi-band jammers covering 70 MHz to 12 GHz and both soft-kill and kinetic hard-kill options designed specifically for swarm and first-person view (FPV) drone threats.

The structural gap, however, is in the reverse direction. India’s EW architecture is currently more capable of attacking adversary drone systems than it is of protecting its own drones from hostile EW operations. Indian UAVs lack hardened, jam-resistant data links and the robust autonomy logic needed for contested electromagnetic environments. The same electromagnetic denial that India is investing in to neutralise enemy drones would, under current conditions, neutralise India’s own drone fleet with comparable effectiveness.

The doctrinal response to this gap has been substantial and reflects a serious institutional recognition of the problem. In 2025, India launched Project Pragyashakti, designed to create a tri-service, AI-driven EW backbone unifying the disparate Army, Navy, and Air Force EW systems under a common operational framework. The project integrates American, Russian, French, and Indian-origin EW equipment via standardised middleware, with machine learning modules for interception, threat detection, waveform decoding, jamming management, electronic counter-countermeasures, and inter-platform data fusion.

The Indian Army’s decision this year to raise dedicated Electronic Warfare Brigades along the Pakistan and China borders, consolidating EW operations previously dispersed across Signals Units, provides the institutional structure to operationalise what Pragyashakti offers at the software layer. The Rs.5,150 crore upgrade to the Dharashakti EW system and the Rs.1,476 crore contract for mobile ground-based EW systems designed to move with combat formations in high-altitude terrain make up the procurement layer. Dharashakti upgrades have demonstrated advanced UAV detection, analysis, and neutralisation at ranges up to 150 km in joint Army-Air Force exercises, with real-time threat assessment and jamming support.

Additionally, the Ministry of Defence’s approval of a Rs.500 crore National Military Drone Technology Hub at IIT Kanpur represents the most direct institutional response to the October 2025 trial failure. The hub’s mandate is specifically oriented towards developing encrypted, frequency-hopping, jam-resistant data links for contested electromagnetic environments, electro-optical targeting systems resilient to EW interference, and multi-layer counter-drone architectures combining passive and active countermeasures. True self-reliance extends beyond final assembly. It requires domestic production of critical parts, including software, engines, and communication systems, to reduce import dependence. This principle applies with particular force to EW-resilient drone communications, where the data link architecture is as strategically critical as the drone platform itself.

The hub’s research outputs will be operationally significant only if they translate into mandatory procurement standards. A jam-resistant, frequency-hopping, encrypted data link must become a non-negotiable baseline requirement for every UAV inducted into the Indian Armed Forces, established through contested-spectrum field trials as a condition of service acceptance. Research excellence at the hub level must be matched by procurement rigour at the acquisition level.

The threat environment against which India must build is not static. Adversaries, specifically China, whose EW capabilities are among the most sophisticated in the world, increasingly employ software-defined radios and cognitive radio architectures capable of identifying and moving away from jamming signals in near real time. Conventional preset-frequency jamming, however powerful, is progressively less effective against systems designed for spectrum agility.

DRDO has identified AI and machine learning for EW applications, including smart jamming against software-defined and cognitive radio systems, as a technology priority within its Electronics and Communication Systems cluster. The operationalisation of that research priority into deployed cognitive EW systems is what separates a 2026-calibre EW architecture from one capable of maintaining electromagnetic relevance through the 2030s.

Electronic and cyber warfare can neutralise most modern weapon systems and precision-guided munitions. The inverse also holds: an adversary’s EW capability can neutralise India’s weapons systems and precision munitions if India’s own systems lack the resilience to operate in contested electromagnetic environments. The campaign that India must mount to close its EW drone resilience gap is not a niche technical programme. It is a foundational requirement for the effective employment of every other capability in India’s autonomous warfare portfolio.

India’s current EW trajectory is one of credible improvement against a widening threat baseline. The investment programme is serious, the doctrinal recognition is genuine, and the institutional architecture, from the EW brigades through Pragyashakti to the IIT Kanpur hub, is broadly appropriate to the problem. The variable that determines whether this trajectory is sufficient is execution speed relative to adversary development pace.

India’s defence preparedness has traditionally prioritised offensive capability over survivability. Drone and missile warfare demand a correction. That correction, in the electromagnetic domain specifically, requires treating the resilience of India’s own UAV fleet and Command and Control or C2 networks as a first-order operational priority rather than a secondary technical concern. The US-Iran conflict demonstrated what sustained drone attrition does to even the best-resourced military in the world. The electromagnetic domain is where the next conflict’s outcome will be substantially shaped, and India’s preparation for that domain must match the urgency of the threat it faces.

Sudhanshu Kumar is a researcher and subject matter expert on AI, Cyberwarfare and Cybersecurity at the Centre for Joint Warfare Studies, Headquarters of the Integrated Defence Staff, Ministry of Defence, New Delhi.
